**The Eight Silver Stitches**

Long before the children went missing, an elf helped a poor shoemaker.

That was how the old story began. The elf came at night, worked by candlelight, and left behind shoes so fine that the shoemaker’s fortunes changed. In most versions, the elf disappeared before anyone could ask his name.

In the family history of **House Silverstitch**, there was another ending.

The elf returned.

Generations later, one of his descendants married into the shoemaker’s family. Their children inherited both gifts: the elf’s knack for enchantment and the shoemaker’s gift for making something beautiful from almost nothing. They built a celebrated shoe house whose work was worn by queens, travelers, and people who needed a little magic in their step.

The family grew wealthy. Their workshops became halls. Their halls became an estate. Their name appeared on royal invitations and the doors of charitable schools.

But there was one part of the family story the Silverstitches never put on display: the elf had left behind **eight silver needles**, each said to hold a different kind of magic. They were passed down through the family, one to each child in every generation.

When the Silverstitch children were young, their mother told them the needles were only a legend.

Their father knew better.

**The Festival of Lanterns**

The eight siblings were still children when they disappeared.

**Elowen**, the eldest, was eleven. **Caelan** was ten, **Maelis** nine, and **Rowan** eight. The younger four—**Thalia**, **Dain**, **Nerys**, and **Orren**—were between seven and three.

Their parents brought them to the Festival of Lanterns in the border town of Briarbridge. It was a grand gathering of merchants, musicians, and visitors from both Elarion and its neighboring kingdom, Veyr. The Silverstitch family had attended every year for generations. Their father sponsored the shoemakers’ pavilion; their mother gave silver coins to the festival’s charitable fund.

That night, all eight children wore little masks shaped like leaves. Each had a silver stitch embroidered at the edge, their mother’s secret mark.

They were supposed to stay near their parents.

They did—until the music stopped.

A hush passed through the crowd, then shouting. Someone cried that a pavilion had caught fire. A group rushed toward the river. Another surged in the opposite direction. The children were swept apart in an instant.

Elowen caught Orren’s hand. Caelan grabbed Nerys. Rowan shouted for Maelis. Someone knocked into Thalia, and the little girl tumbled beneath a table. In the confusion, a woman in a green festival cloak appeared beside her.

“I know where your brother is,” she said.

Thalia believed her.

The woman led her away from the crowd, toward a covered wagon. Inside, other frightened children huddled together. A boy sobbed that he couldn’t find his mother. Another held a broken festival lantern.

The woman promised to take them somewhere safe.

By the time the Silverstitch parents realized all eight children were gone, the wagon had crossed into Veyr.

The festival had not been a rescue.

It had been a harvest.

**The House of Good Beginnings**

The children were taken to an orphanage called **The House of Good Beginnings**. Its sign showed a smiling sun above a yellow door. Its director, Mistress Vale, wore clean dresses and spoke softly to visiting merchants.

Inside, the children were hungry, frightened, and told they had no families.

Mistress Vale renamed them. She said it was kinder than letting them remember the people who had abandoned them.

The staff separated the siblings within days.

Elowen protested and was locked in a storage room until she learned to stay quiet. Caelan was sent to the laundry and kitchen to work. Maelis was made to entertain visitors with songs. Rowan was assigned to carry messages between the orphanage and its wealthy patrons. Thalia, Dain, and Nerys were placed in crowded dormitories. Little Orren was kept close to Mistress Vale because he had noticed that some children left the home and never came back.

The orphanage traded children under the names of apprenticeships, household placements, and charitable adoptions. The money bought silk curtains, imported wine, and a private garden for Mistress Vale. The children who remained were made to work for their meals. If they asked after one another, they were punished or told their siblings had already been sent away.

One night, Elowen managed to slip into the laundry room. She found seven small scraps of fabric in a basket, each marked with a silver stitch.

She hid them beneath a loose floorboard.

By morning, the scraps were gone.

Years later, she could not remember whether they had been real.

**The Same Kingdom, Different Lives**

The siblings grew up in Veyr, but none of them grew up together.

Some were moved from place to place. Others escaped. A few were sent to households that treated them well enough to keep them quiet. As they became adults, they built separate lives in the capital and the nearby river towns.

They were close enough to pass one another without knowing it.

Elowen became an assistant healer. Once, she treated a young blacksmith who had burned his palm. Caelan thanked her with a pair of shoes he had repaired himself. Neither noticed that both had the same tiny crescent-shaped scar beside the thumb.

Maelis sang in the market square. Thalia often stopped to listen while selling maps across the street. The singer’s melody felt familiar, but Thalia couldn’t say why.

Rowan joined the city guard. He once helped Dain unload a boat after a storm, then escorted him away when the harbor master accused him of smuggling. They argued all the way to the gate and parted without learning each other’s names.

Nerys sold flowers outside the archive where Orren worked as a copyist. She always left one white blossom on the stone windowsill. Orren never knew who brought them. He kept every one between the pages of a book about old elven craft.

Sometimes they dreamed of eight children running through a festival crowd.

Sometimes they heard the same lullaby in a stranger’s voice.

Sometimes, in a crowded street, they turned because someone had called a name they had not heard since childhood.

For a long time, they thought these were only fragments of dreams.

**The Story Beneath the Story**

The Silverstitch parents searched every town in Elarion first. They questioned merchants, paid for notices, and sent riders down every road. When they learned the children might have crossed into Veyr, they expanded the search—but every trail ended at a false name, a burned ledger, or a witness who suddenly remembered nothing.

They spent a fortune on investigators. They offered rewards. They visited orphanages, hospitals, workshops, and city offices. They returned to Briarbridge every year, even after the festival stopped feeling like a celebration.

Their family wealth opened doors, but it could not tell them what names their children had been given.

It took them years to discover the orphanage had been involved. It took longer still to prove that their children had survived it. The House of Good Beginnings kept two sets of books: one for public inspections and one for the children who had been sold or placed in private homes. Mistress Vale had hidden the second set inside a wall before fleeing Veyr.

It would take the siblings even longer to discover who they were.

Their first real clue appeared in the archive.

Orren was repairing a torn book about the old shoemaker when he found a narrow strip of silver stitched into its binding. The thread warmed beneath his fingers. On the page beside it, a line of writing appeared that had not been there before:

**Eight were lost beneath eight lanterns. Eight must choose their own road home.**

Orren took the book to the market to ask whether anyone recognized the stitching.

Nerys saw it first.

Her flower basket slipped from her hands.

Across the square, Maelis stopped singing. Caelan stepped out of his workshop. Rowan pushed through the crowd, one hand on his sword. Thalia hurried over from her map stall. Dain tied his boat and came running. Elowen, carrying a healer’s bag, stared at the silver thread as if it had spoken her name.

None of them knew why they had come.

None of them knew one another.

Then the archive book opened by itself. A tiny silver needle rolled from its spine and stopped at the feet of the youngest-looking man.

Orren picked it up.

Every bell in the city rang once.

Far away, in Elarion, the Silverstitch parents heard the same note. Their oldest investigator—who had spent most of his life following vanished children—ran into their chambers carrying a sealed ledger recovered from Veyr.

On its first page were eight names.

Not the names the siblings had grown up with.

Their birth names.

The parents had finally found the truth.

But someone in Veyr had spent years making sure the children would never find it for themselves. And the person who stole the silver needle from the book was already on the way to the market.

**The Shoes That Remembered**

The royal gathering was meant to be remembered as the happiest night of the year.

Lanterns hung from the palace balconies. Musicians played in the crowded square, and the king and queen walked among their guests without the usual crown guards pressing close. It was the Festival of the First Stitch, held each year to honor the old shoemaker whose cleverness had once saved his family from poverty.

The royal children had heard the story since they were small. Long ago, their ancestor had been a humble shoemaker. When he and his wife were struggling, mysterious little elves had secretly made beautiful shoes in his workshop. The shoemaker had never forgotten their kindness. He had promised that his family would always protect the elves’ secret and repay their help if the day ever came.

But the promise had been forgotten by nearly everyone.

During the festival, a traveling shoemaker displayed a pair of tiny silver shoes beneath a glass bell. They were said to be made by the elves themselves. The children pressed close to see them—and in the crush of the crowd, they were swept apart from their parents.

A woman in a gray cloak took them by the hands.

“Your parents are looking for you,” she whispered. “I’ll bring you to them.”

She did not.

By dawn, the children had been carried across the border into another kingdom. Their names were scratched from the travel ledger. Their fine festival clothes were replaced with rough garments, and they were delivered to an orphanage that called itself a refuge.

It was no refuge.

The master of the orphanage kept the children hungry and afraid. Some were sent away to work in distant houses. Others were traded to wealthy patrons in exchange for jewels, fine food, and favors from the royal court. The master insisted the children had no families and no pasts worth remembering.

But the siblings did remember things.

One remembered their mother humming the festival song. Another remembered the smell of their father’s leather workshop. The youngest kept drawing a pair of silver shoes, though no one had ever shown them those shoes.

And sometimes, when the orphanage was quiet, the children heard tiny footsteps beneath the floorboards.

Years passed. The king and queen never stopped searching. They sent riders across the kingdoms, questioned merchants, and offered rewards for any clue about their missing children. Their wealth opened many doors, but it could not open the one hiding the truth: the orphanage’s master had powerful friends.

A rival noble family was helping him.

That family claimed descent from the shoemaker, too. They wanted the royal family’s place—and believed that if the missing children were never found, their own claim to the old elf magic could be made to seem true. They had spent years collecting little treasures from the orphanage: a child’s ribbon, a broken toy, a button from a festival coat. They did not know that each object held a memory.

The first clue came from a cracked wooden button.

A girl who had once lived at the orphanage found it behind a loose stone in the cellar. When she touched it, she heard music—not the song playing in the cellar, but the festival music from years earlier. She saw lanterns, a crowded square, and a woman in a gray cloak leading children away.

Then the vision vanished.

The button had remembered.

Before she could show anyone, a boy arrived at the orphanage with a bundle of old shoes. He was a quiet apprentice, hired to repair the children’s worn footwear. He kept his sleeves buttoned at the wrists and avoided the master’s eyes. But one night, the girl saw him mend a shoe without needle or thread. A soft green light curled around his fingers.

He was an elf.

Or he had been. The orphanage master had stolen the little silver tool that held his magic, and without it, the boy could not return to his people. He had hidden among humans for years, searching for the children who had vanished on the festival night.

He knew the family’s old promise. He knew the siblings were alive.

And he knew that someone had been using the old magic to erase children’s identities—and the orphanage might only be one part of it.

And he knew the elves had been watching.

Deep in the northern woods, beyond a path that appeared only at moonrise, stood the hidden village of the elves. They remembered the shoemaker and the debt his family had sworn to repay. They also remembered that someone had broken into their workshop generations later and stolen the pattern for making enchanted shoes.

The stolen pattern had been used to create one extraordinary pair.

The shoes could find lost people. They could cross locked doors and unmarked borders. And when they touched the ground, they left no footprints—only a faint silver shimmer that could be seen by the person they were meant to find.

The pair had been separated. One shoe was kept by the rival noble family as a symbol of their supposed inheritance. The other had been hidden in the orphanage’s cellar, where the master stored the belongings of children he had sold away.

When the siblings finally touched the shoes again, the leather warmed beneath their hands.

A voice—soft as a whisper from a long-forgotten room—rose from within them.

“Find one another,” it said.

The siblings did not yet know who they truly were. They did not know their parents had spent years searching. They did not know the elves were watching from the forest, or that the rival family had already learned they might be alive.

But the shoes remembered.

And somewhere across the kingdom, their mother heard the old festival song in a dream for the first time in years. At the very end of it, a child’s voice sang the missing line:

*Follow the silver where the lost ones go.*

The king woke beside her.

Neither of them spoke. They were already reaching for their cloaks.

**Part II: The Road Beneath the Forest**

By sunrise, the king and queen were on the road.

They did not ride with a parade or announce their search. They took only two trusted guards and the old festival singer, whose memory for songs was better than any royal record keeper’s. The queen carried a faded ribbon from one child’s festival coat. The king carried a map marked with every town they had searched before.

They had searched for years. They had followed false sightings, bribed dishonest officials, and questioned travelers who remembered children with their eyes or their smiles. Each lead had ended in disappointment. Now, for the first time, they had a clue that seemed to come from the children themselves.

At the orphanage, the girl with the wooden button had no idea the king and queen were coming.

She kept the button hidden in her pocket. Whenever she touched it, she heard a few notes of the festival song and saw the same image: a woman in a gray cloak leading children through the crowd. The woman’s face was always blurred. So was the face of the person who had pointed her toward the children.

That missing detail bothered her most.

The button showed the children being led away. It never showed who had sent them.

“You’re trying to make the memory say more than it can,” the young shoemaker told her.

He had been mending shoes in the corner of the cellar. He spoke softly and kept his head down whenever the orphanage master passed. The girl knew he was hiding something. She had seen the green light around his fingers, and she had found the little silver tool he wore beneath his shirt.

“You know about the button,” she said.

“I know it remembers,” he replied. “But it was made by elves. Memories don’t always arrive in the order we want them to.”

“What are you?”

For a moment, the young man stopped stitching.

“An elf,” he said. “Or I was, before I lost my magic.”

The little silver tool had once been part of an elf’s craft set. It was called a **Silver Last**—a tool used to shape shoes, but also to shape paths. In the right hands, it could make a road appear where no road existed. It could open a locked door, carry a message across kingdoms, or guide a lost person home.

The elf had carried it when he was a child. A few nights after the festival, someone stole it. Without it, his magic faded. He had been searching ever since for the thief—and for the children who had disappeared that night.

“I saw them taken,” he confessed. “I was supposed to help them. I failed.”

The girl studied his face. “You saw us?”

“I saw children being led away. I didn’t know who you were then. I was young, frightened, and looking for the Silver Last. By the time I understood what was happening, the carriage was gone.”

He had kept one secret from her: he had recognized the queen’s ribbon on the girl’s coat. He had suspected she was one of the missing royals from the beginning. But the orphanage master had powerful allies, and the elf had feared that revealing the truth too soon would place every child in danger.

That evening, the girl found the shoes.

They were tucked beneath a broken cabinet in the orphanage’s storeroom: one small silver shoe, delicate as a leaf, with a worn sole and a tiny star stitched into the heel. She had seen it before—or thought she had. It had appeared beside her bed once, then vanished when the master came to inspect the room.

Now it rested beneath the cabinet as if it had been waiting for her.

The moment she touched it, the air turned cold.

She saw the festival again. This time, the crowd parted around a small display of shoes beneath a glass bell. A woman in gray led the children away. Then the memory jumped. The image changed to a noblewoman watching from a balcony, a gold ring shining on her hand.

The girl gasped. The vision disappeared before she could see the woman’s face.

The shoe had remembered more than the button, but not everything.

The young elf examined it. “This is one of the shoemaker’s shoes.”

“Your shoemaker?” she asked.

“Our shoemaker,” he replied. “His family was human, but he was the first person to help us when we had nowhere safe to go.”

He told her the story the orphanage master had tried to bury.

Long ago, when the elves had helped the poor shoemaker, he had promised to protect their hidden village and keep their secret. In return, the elves gave him the gift of making shoes that could find the lost and open paths through locked doors. The gift passed down through his family—but it slept until the family stood together again.

The shoemaker had also made another promise.

One of the elves had been in danger. The shoemaker sheltered the elf and helped him return to his people. In gratitude, the elves had given him the Silver Last. He swore that if it were ever stolen and used to harm the innocent, his descendants would help return it and restore the hidden road between the kingdoms.

For generations, the promise had gone unneeded.

Now the Silver Last was missing, the hidden road was closing, and children’s names were being erased.

The orphanage master was not working alone. A wealthy family called House Vale had given him money, fine clothes, and protection from questions. House Vale claimed that it, too, descended from the shoemaker. Its leaders insisted that the royal family had stolen their rightful place in the line of inheritance.

They wanted more than the throne.

They wanted the elf magic.

With the Silver Last, the orphanage master could alter records, confuse memories, and make children disappear into new lives. He called it a business. House Vale called it a way to erase the royal children and secure its claim forever.

Some children had been sent away to work. Others had been sold to wealthy households. Their names had been crossed out of books, and their memories had been blurred by the stolen magic. The orphanage was only one part of a much larger scheme.

“We have to get the Silver Last back,” the girl said.

The elf shook his head. “You don’t understand. If we follow the shoes to the elves before you’re ready, the hidden village will be exposed.”

“Then tell me what I’m not ready for.”

He looked away. “The elves warned me that the shoemaker’s descendants would return. They said that when the children were found, the family reunion must wait.”

“Wait for what?”

“For the danger to pass.”

The girl frowned. “That sounds like something people say when they want you to stay frightened.”

Before he could answer, a bell rang upstairs.

The orphanage master was coming down.

The elf grabbed the girl’s hand. The silver shoe glimmered. A narrow seam appeared in the cellar wall, widening into a doorway that had not been there before.

They slipped through just as the master entered.

The doorway closed behind them.

On the other side was a moonlit forest.

Far away, the king and queen had reached the town where the orphanage stood. They did not know their daughter was already outside its walls. They did not know the old festival singer had recognized the tune carved into the ribbon’s clasp.

The song’s missing line was not merely a clue. It was a map.

“Follow the silver where the lost ones go,” the singer repeated. “That is not the whole line. There’s another verse.”

The queen closed her eyes and sang the tune from memory. Her voice trembled, but the old words came back:

*Where the first stitch crossed the stream,*\
&#x20;*Where the moonlight hid the seam,*\
&#x20;*Follow silver, follow true,*\
&#x20;*The lost road waits for all of you.*

The royal family had not simply vanished into another kingdom. They had crossed the hidden path the shoemaker had once opened—and someone had closed it behind them.

The king looked toward the forest.

“Then that’s where we go,” he said.

But House Vale had already learned of their arrival.

That night, its matriarch opened a locked room beneath her estate. Inside stood a desk covered in children’s records, a silver tool, and a row of small objects taken from the orphanage: a button, a ribbon, a wooden horse, and a child’s first shoe.

She touched the Silver Last to the pages.

Names faded.

Faces slipped from memory.

Yet when she reached for the queen’s ribbon, the tool gave a sharp, bright spark. The ribbon would not lose its memory.

The matriarch’s expression hardened.

“They’ve started remembering,” she whispered.

At the forest’s edge, the girl’s silver shoe began to glow. A second shoe appeared in the path ahead of them. It was larger, scuffed, and familiar to the elf.

“My Silver Last,” he said, staring at it.

The stolen tool had taken the shape of a shoe.

It had been moving from place to place, following the scattered children, waiting for the family to come close enough to awaken it. The girl picked it up. The young elf’s hands shook as he reached for it, but he stopped himself.

“It belongs to you,” she said.

“It belongs to the elves.”

“Then we’ll take it back together.”

The shoes turned toward the trees.

For the first time, they did more than show a path. They began to walk—though no feet were inside them. Their silver heels tapped across the earth, leaving shining footprints that led into the dark.

The girl followed.

The elf followed her.

And somewhere behind them, beyond the orphanage and the road, a boy who shared her eyes woke from a dream of lanterns and music. He remembered a woman singing the festival song. He remembered a silver shoe beneath a glass bell.

Most of all, he remembered a name that no one at the orphanage had ever called him.

As the siblings drew closer, the shoes’ hidden magic stirred.

But the forest was listening.

A soft voice came from among the trees.

“Stop,” it warned. “If you bring the children to the elves before you know who is erasing their names, the hidden village will fall.”

The elf stepped in front of the girl.

From the shadows emerged a circle of small figures with pale green cloaks. Their faces were watchful, and their hands held tiny lanterns that burned with blue flame.

The elves had been watching the missing children for years.

Their leader looked at the silver shoes, then at the girl.

“The old promise is coming due,” she said. “But first, you must learn what your ancestor promised us—and what House Vale intends to do with the Silver Last.”

The girl glanced at the path behind her. Somewhere out there were her brothers and sisters. Somewhere beyond them, her parents were still searching.

“Then tell me,” she said. “And don’t leave out the part everyone keeps hiding.”

The elf leader lowered her lantern.

“I will tell you,” she said. “But the memory you seek belongs to the one person you have not yet found.”

And deep inside the forest, a bell rang once.

**Part III: The Memory No One Could Keep**

The bell’s note traveled through the trees.

It did not fade the way an ordinary bell would. It passed through the branches and under the ground, making the leaves tremble. The blue flames in the elves’ lanterns bent toward the sound.

The girl felt the wooden button grow warm in her pocket.

The elf leader looked at it. “You brought a memory with you.”

“It belonged to a child at the orphanage,” the girl said. “I found it in the cellar.”

The leader’s face changed. “Then the cellar is older than we feared.”

She led them away from the path. The elves walked without snapping a twig or stirring the moss. Their lanterns showed no road ahead, yet every time the girl blinked, the trees had shifted and the group had moved farther into the forest.

The silver shoes walked alongside them.

The girl kept glancing back at the young elf. He was free of the orphanage now, but the little tool beneath his shirt still glowed faintly, like an ember nearly gone.

“Can you get your magic back?” she asked.

“Maybe,” he said. “If the Silver Last returns to the village.”

“Then why did you stop me from taking it?”

“Because the elves’ warning was real. Someone is using the old craft to erase names. If we rush into the village, House Vale may follow the trail.”

The girl frowned. “They already know we’re remembering.”

“Yes,” the leader said. “And they know the hidden road has begun to wake.”

The trees opened onto a narrow stream. Its water reflected a sky full of stars, though the sky above the forest was clouded. On the far bank stood a stone arch covered in tiny carved shoes. Some were polished smooth; others were chipped or cracked.

“Where the first stitch crossed the stream,” the elf leader said.

The girl recognized the words from the festival song.

The silver shoes stepped into the water. Instead of sinking, they walked across its surface, leaving shining ripples behind them. The elf leader raised her lantern, and a doorway appeared inside the stone arch.

Beyond it lay the hidden village.

It was smaller than the girl expected, but it seemed to stretch farther than the eye could follow. Houses had been built into tree trunks and beneath hillsides. Windows glowed like fireflies. Bridges of woven grass connected the rooftops. In the center of the village stood a workshop with a dark, empty doorway.

The elves fell silent as they approached it.

“That was the shoemaker’s workshop?” the girl asked.

“It was where he made the first pair,” the leader answered. “And where he made his promise.”

She took the girl inside.

On the workbench lay the outline of a shoe, carved into the wood. Beside it was a message written in the old stitching marks of the shoemaker’s family. The girl could not read the marks, but her fingers moved over them as if they recognized the pattern.

The elf leader began to translate:

“*When my house stands divided, let the shoes keep the road. When my blood is lost, let the silver seek it. When names are stolen, let my children give them back.*”

The girl pulled away from the workbench. “That’s what my ancestor promised?”

“Part of it,” said the leader. “He promised that his family would help the elves protect the hidden road. The road joins our village to the human kingdoms. It is more than a shortcut. It lets memories, names, and messages travel safely between our peoples.”

“And House Vale is using the Silver Last to close it?”

“They are using it to control who can cross,” the leader replied. “They believe that if they can erase the royal children from memory, they can make the kingdom accept their claim. But the Silver Last is not meant to erase. It was made to shape a path.”

The girl thought of the faces in the visions—the blurred woman, the shadow on the balcony, the figure who had pointed toward the children.

“Who was the person who sent us away?”

The elf leader did not answer at once.

“The memories are incomplete,” she said. “A memory object cannot show what its maker did not understand. The person who saw the children taken was too young to know who gave the order.”

The girl turned toward the young elf.

“You said you were there.”

He nodded, shame darkening his face.

“I saw someone point the woman in gray toward the children. I thought it was a festival attendant. I didn’t know they were being taken.”

“Do you remember who it was?”

“No. I’ve tried. The Silver Last was stolen soon after, and my memories of that night became tangled. I only remember the ring.”

“The gold ring,” the girl said.

The elf leader’s eyes narrowed. “Then the memory is beginning to join itself.”

The village bell rang a second time.

This time, a figure emerged from the workshop’s far doorway.

She was small, wrapped in a dark green cloak. Her hair was silver-white, though her face looked young. In one hand she held a tiny hammer. In the other, a little shoe made from dark leather.

The elf leader bowed her head.

“Keeper,” she said.

The newcomer looked directly at the girl. “You have been asking for the missing memory.”

“Who are you?”

“I was the one who sent the woman in gray toward your family.”

The girl went still.

The young elf stepped forward. “You?”

“I was a child,” the Keeper said. “I saw House Vale’s agent moving through the festival. I thought the woman was returning the children to their parents. I pointed her toward them because she said she was helping.”

“Why didn’t you tell anyone?”

“I did. No one believed me. By the time I understood what had happened, the children were gone and the Silver Last had been stolen. House Vale’s magic blurred my memory. I remembered the children, but not the face of the person who gave the order.”

The girl touched the wooden button.

The Keeper’s words seemed to settle into it. The button warmed and gave a faint click.

A new image opened in the air above the workbench: the festival square, the woman in gray, and a noblewoman on the balcony. This time the gold ring was clear. Its stone was shaped like a closed eye.

The Keeper drew in a sharp breath. “That ring belonged to House Vale’s matriarch.”

The girl watched as the memory shifted. The matriarch leaned toward a man beside her and whispered. He pointed toward the children. The woman in gray moved into the crowd.

The missing detail had finally appeared.

But the vision did not stop there. It showed the woman in gray guiding the children through a side gate, where the orphanage master waited. Then the image broke apart into flashes: a carriage, a signet ring, a ledger, and one child being carried in the opposite direction from the others.

The girl reached toward the memory.

“Wait,” she said. “One of us was separated before we reached the orphanage.”

The Keeper’s face turned pale.

The elf leader closed her lantern’s glass cover. “The memory has shown what it can.”

“Where is that child?” the girl demanded.

“We don’t know,” said the Keeper. “The child was taken somewhere else.”

The bell rang a third time, so loudly that the workshop shook.

Across the village, a line of silver light appeared on the ground. It ran from the stone arch, through the workshop, and toward the forest beyond.

The silver shoes turned toward it.

The elf stared down at his hands. A green glow had returned to his fingertips.

“The road is opening,” he whispered.

The girl looked at the elves. “Then help me find my siblings.”

The leader shook her head. “The family gift has not fully awakened. The shoes can lead you toward the lost, but they cannot reveal every danger. Until your siblings stand together again, House Vale can still twist the road.”

“Then we find them before House Vale does.”

At that moment, in a distant estate, the boy from the dream sat up in bed.

He was no longer at the orphanage. He had been sold to a wealthy household years ago and taught to answer to a name that was not his own. He had never known the other children were his siblings. He had never been told that his parents were still searching.

But on his bedside table stood a small silver shoe.

It had appeared there sometime during the night.

A trail of light led from its toe to the locked door.

The boy rose, put on his coat, and touched the shoe.

From somewhere beyond the walls, a voice called the name he had forgotten.

This time, he remembered it.

And the shoe opened the door.
